AUGM: Large US stocks with the maximum available buffer over each year starting in August, built to absorb as much of any loss as the options allow, in exchange for a low cap on gains. Maximum protection is the point; in a strong year it will finish far behind the market.
AVGB: Investment-grade bonds from companies, governments and agencies around the world, hedged back into dollars, chosen with a tilt toward bonds offering better expected returns. It's a core bond holding with more corporate credit than Treasury-heavy rivals, so it pays a bit more and dips more in credit panics.
AVRY: A focused portfolio of US growth companies, many of them mid-sized technology and software firms rather than giants, picked by active managers. With half in technology and a short list of names, it swings more than broad funds and lives or dies by its stock picking.
BFLB: Large US stocks through options, with a preset amount of loss protection built in and the level set dynamically by the manager. It's an actively run buffer fund rather than a fixed formula, so the protection and caps can change as the manager adjusts the options.
BKF: Companies from just three big emerging markets: Brazil, India and China, led by Chinese internet giants and banks from all three countries. It's a concentrated slice of the emerging world, so its fate rides on those three economies and currencies, not the broader group.
BOTT: Companies building humanoid and service robots and the parts inside them, from motors and sensors to full machines, spread across China, the US and elsewhere. It's a bet on robots entering factories and daily life, a young industry where stocks are speculative and swing hard.
BSMZ: Investment-grade municipal bonds all maturing in 2035, in a fund that wraps up at the end of that year, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. Like a single long-term muni bond, it suits money aimed at a 2035 goal, and its price swings with interest rates until then.
CAMX: Twenty to thirty companies from the US and abroad that the manager judges the best value opportunities, spread across health care, industrials, media and consumer names. 'Aggressive' means concentrated and willing to swing: a short list of strong opinions rather than a diversified market basket.
CEFA: Companies in developed markets outside the US, screened to align with Catholic values, leaving out businesses tied to abortion, certain weapons and other activities the Church opposes. Financials lead the mix; it's a faith-based core overseas holding, otherwise similar in shape to a broad foreign fund.
CLNK: A trust holding Chainlink, the token of a network that feeds real-world data like prices into blockchains, so its value follows that one cryptocurrency. It gives stock-market access to a smaller, more speculative coin than bitcoin, and it can swing even harder than the big cryptocurrencies.
CSSD: Preferred shares and similar income securities chosen for short maturities and investment-grade quality, mostly from big banks in the US and abroad. Short duration is the point: it pays preferred-style income with less price movement when interest rates change than most preferred funds.
DMXU: Large and mid-sized companies across developed markets outside North America, in Europe, Japan, Australia and elsewhere, led by banks, technology and industrial firms. It's a core overseas holding with one twist: it leaves out Canada as well as the US, so North America is absent entirely.
DVAL: Large US companies trading at value prices, led by banks at nearly a third, with a dynamic approach that shifts between flavors of value as conditions change. It's an active core value holding; the shifting style means it won't always behave like a plain cheap-stock fund.
ECNS: Small Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong, spread across health care, technology, industrials and consumer names, with no single giant dominating. Small caps in China are a wilder ride than the famous internet giants: less researched, more exposed to local policy, and quick to swing on sentiment.
EGGS: Growth stocks, mostly technology, paired with an options portfolio meant to generate income and guard against large market declines. The guard is the idea: it gives up some upside to options in exchange for a hedge, aiming for a smoother total return than the stocks alone would give.
ENZL: New Zealand companies, led by a medical device maker and infrastructure and airport firms, with health care and industrials together over half the fund. It's a tiny, concentrated market where a handful of companies dominate, so it moves gently most days but hinges on a few names.
EPRF: Investment-grade preferred shares, almost all from financial companies like banks and asset managers, paying fixed dividends ahead of common stockholders. It's a steadier income holding than most preferred funds because it skips junk-rated issuers, though it still falls when interest rates rise or banks wobble.
EUDG: European companies chosen for growing their dividends while staying profitable, spread across industrial firms, banks, drug makers and consumer brands. It's a quality-and-income take on Europe for the core of a portfolio, calmer than most stock funds but still fully exposed when markets fall.
FCSH: Short-term corporate bonds from investment-grade companies, mostly big banks and other large firms, kept on short maturities to limit price swings. It's a steadier income holding a step riskier than Treasury funds, paying a bit more interest in exchange for company credit risk.
FXC: Simply Canadian dollars held in a deposit account, wrapped so they trade like a stock. It's a direct bet on the currency: it gains when the Canadian dollar strengthens against the US dollar and loses when it weakens, with no stocks or bonds inside at all.
HXF: A managed futures strategy that trades trends and big economic themes across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long or short as signals dictate. It's a hedge-fund style diversifier meant to zig when portfolios zag, and it can lose money in trendless, choppy markets when signals keep flipping.
IBAT: Companies working on storing energy: battery makers, hydrogen and fuel cell firms, industrial gas giants and the materials suppliers behind them. It's a bet on the build-out behind electric vehicles and renewable power, spread globally, and it swings with clean-energy enthusiasm.
IJUN: Large companies in developed markets outside the US, combined with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in June, in exchange for a cap on gains. Banks and industrial firms are the biggest slice overseas; the year resets every June, so timing within it matters.
ITDG: A retirement fund for people planning to retire around 2055, currently invested almost entirely in US and overseas stocks for growth. It will shift toward bonds gradually over the coming decades, putting a whole lifetime investing plan into a single holding that adjusts itself.
IWFG: A focused portfolio of large growth companies, with technology over half the fund and its biggest position an unusually large share. Winslow's managers pick a short list of durable growers, so concentration is the point: it can pull well ahead of the market or fall well behind it.
KAUG: Small US companies with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in August, in exchange for a cap on gains. The cushion is the draw, since small stocks swing hard; in a strong small-cap rally the cap will leave it behind plain small-cap funds.
KNGZ: Large US companies with long records of stable or rising dividends, diversified so no single industry dominates, though older technology names paying dividends are the biggest slice here. It's an income-leaning core holding built on dependable payers rather than the highest yields.
KWIN: US growth stocks, heavily technology, screened to comply with Islamic finance principles, in a fund designed to produce income in a Shariah-consistent way. The screen rules out conventional banks and interest-heavy businesses, leaving a tech-heavy portfolio that swings like a growth fund despite the income goal.
KWT: Kuwaiti companies, dominated by banks at about two-thirds of the fund, with real estate, phone and industrial firms far behind. It's an extremely concentrated single-country fund where two big banks drive most of the result, so it behaves more like a bet on Kuwaiti banking than a broad market.
LCR: A tactical mix of stock, bond and commodity funds adjusted by the manager's market research, able to shift defensive and even hold a fund that gains when stocks fall. It's a core holding for investors who want someone else steering through cycles, and it will trail in long bull runs.
LQDI: Investment-grade corporate bonds, combined with inflation swaps meant to cancel out the damage inflation does to bond prices. It's an income holding for investors worried about inflation: the hedge protects purchasing power, though it can drag on returns when inflation cools.
MAGG: The broad US investment-grade bond market in one fund: Treasury bonds, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate debt, actively managed around a benchmark-like mix. It's a core bond holding for steady income and ballast against stock drops, and it still falls when interest rates rise.
NDEC: The big growth companies of the Nasdaq, technology about three-fifths, with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in December, in exchange for a cap on gains. It softens the growth-stock ride, though the cap means a booming year for tech will leave it behind.
NSIG: Large US growth companies picked by an active manager, with technology nearly three-fifths of the fund and a handful of giant positions at the top. It's an aggressive growth holding: the concentrated tech bet can outrun the market in tech-led rallies and fall harder when they reverse.
OVF: Overseas stocks held through broad foreign funds, with an options overlay that sells put options to add extra income on top. The overlay is the twist: it boosts the payout in calm markets but adds losses when overseas stocks fall sharply, so it is not a defensive fund.
PBJA: Large US stocks with a buffer designed to absorb the first fifth of any loss over each year starting in January, in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms reset every January, so the later in the year you buy, the more of the buffer may already be used.
POW: Companies electrifying the world's power systems: grid equipment, transformers, cables and power utilities, mostly industrial firms from around the globe. It's a bet on the electricity supercycle driven by data centers and electric vehicles, so it moves with infrastructure spending more than the broad market.
PSTR: US stock market sectors held through sector funds, rotated toward whichever industries the manager favors, with technology the largest slice right now. The rotation is the strategy: it aims to ride leading sectors and dodge laggards, though mistimed switches can leave it behind the plain market.
PXI: Energy companies chosen by momentum, meaning whichever oil, gas and pipeline stocks have been rising most strongly, from refiners to producers. Energy is already the market's swing sector; the momentum tilt makes this version swing even harder, chasing winners and dropping laggards as trends change.
PYZ: Basic materials companies chosen by momentum: steel makers, chemical firms, miners and fertilizer producers whose stocks have been rising most strongly. Materials swing with global growth and commodity prices, and the momentum tilt makes this fund chase the hottest corner of an already cyclical sector.
QCOC: The Nasdaq's big growth companies with a conservative buffer over each year starting in October, absorbing a larger part of any loss than standard buffer funds, in exchange for a lower cap on gains. Technology is about three-fifths, so the cushion matters: growth stocks swing hard even buffered.
SEMG: Large US growth companies with records of steady earnings growth, picked through a disciplined process, with technology just under half the fund. It's a quality-growth core holding: smoother than aggressive growth funds in exchange for missing some of the wildest rallies in speculative names.
SIXZ: Large US stocks with a buffer over six-month periods starting each May and November, built to absorb roughly the first tenth of any loss in exchange for a cap on gains. Two resets a year keep the shield fresher than annual buffer funds, though a fast drop can still use it up early.
STXD: Large and mid-sized growth companies that also pay dividends, led by technology and banks, screened from the growth side of the market. It blends growth with income for a core holding, which means a lower payout than pure dividend funds but more growth potential than most of them.
SYZ: Small US companies held in a very broad, systematic portfolio, scored on data rather than picked by hand, with technology and industrials the largest slices. No single stock matters much, which makes it a diversified small-cap building block rather than a stock picker's bet.
VBCA: Corporate bonds that all mature around 2027, from banks, phone companies and other large firms, in a fund that wraps up at the end of that year. It behaves like one big bond with a known end date, paying interest along the way and returning principal as bonds mature.
VBCC: Corporate bonds that all mature around 2029, from banks, software firms and other large companies, in a fund that wraps up at the end of that year. Like owning one big bond, it pays interest to a known finish line, making it a tool for money needed around 2029.
XBOC: Large US stocks with a speed boost and a small cushion: over each year starting in October, gains count at an accelerated rate up to a cap, while a modest buffer absorbs the first part of any loss. The faster upside is the draw, and the cap means a huge rally pays only so much.
XSHD: About sixty small US companies chosen for high dividends and historically calmer prices, led by property trusts at about two-fifths. It's an income play in small-cap land: the low-volatility screen softens the usual small-stock swings, though small companies still fall hard in recessions.
ZDIS: Fast-growing 'discovery' companies, businesses the manager believes are early in long growth runs, spread across technology, industrials and consumer names. It's a high-conviction growth fund that buys tomorrow's leaders while they are still proving themselves, so it can swing far more than the broad market.
